items.prompt: Why does a lizard bask in the sun each morning?

options.label: To take in heat its body cannot generate on its own
options.feedback: Basking is exactly this — pulling in outside warmth to replace the internal furnace a lizard does not have.

options.label: To dry raindrops off its scales
options.feedback: A lizard's scales shed water without any special drying ritual; the sun is not needed for that.

options.label: To signal to other lizards that it is awake
options.feedback: Posture, color and movement carry signals between lizards; sitting still in the sun sends no message on its own.

options.label: To get vitamin D from the light for its bones alone
options.feedback: Sunlight does trigger vitamin D in the skin, but that is a side effect, not the reason a cold lizard rushes to bask first thing.

items.ok_line: It has no internal furnace, so it borrows the sun's.
items.ko_line: Think about what a lizard's body cannot do for itself.
items.exp_text: A lizard's own tissues release very little heat as they work, unlike a mammal's, so its body temperature simply follows whatever warms or cools around it. By lying in direct sunlight it absorbs radiant heat through its skin far faster than it could ever produce on its own, and its temperature climbs toward whatever level lets its muscles and nerves work best. Until that happens, a lizard fresh from a cold night is too sluggish to hunt or flee.

items.prompt: Why do a lizard's muscles work poorly on a cold morning?

options.label: The muscles have run out of water overnight
options.feedback: Dehydration weakens muscle over time, but that is not what a single cool night does.

options.label: The chemical reactions that power muscle contraction slow down in the cold
options.feedback: Every contraction depends on chemical reactions, and cold slows chemistry down before it slows anything else.

options.label: Its bones stiffen when the temperature drops
options.feedback: Bone is not sensitive to temperature this way; nothing structural changes overnight.

options.label: It is holding still to hide from predators
options.feedback: Stillness can be a choice, but a chilled lizard often cannot move fast even if it tries to flee.

items.ok_line: Cold chemistry, not a cold decision.
items.ko_line: The cause is inside the cells, not the bones or the water.
items.exp_text: Muscle contraction is driven by chemical reactions inside each fiber, and like most chemical reactions, they run faster when warm and slower when cold. On a cool morning a lizard's whole body sits near the outside temperature, so these reactions crawl and its strikes, sprints and even simple steps lag behind what the same muscles could do once the sun has had time to work on them. A basking lizard is not merely comfortable; it is recharging the speed of its own body.

items.prompt: How does a lizard keep from overheating on a hot afternoon after basking all morning?

options.label: It stops breathing for a while
options.feedback: Breathing continues regardless of temperature; holding it would not cool the body.

options.label: It sheds its outer skin immediately
options.feedback: Shedding happens on its own schedule for growth, not as an on-demand cooling switch.

options.label: It moves into shade or shelter to lose the extra heat
options.feedback: Retreating out of direct sun lets the body cool back down by the same route it warmed up.

options.label: It pants like a dog to release heat
options.feedback: Some reptiles do pant in extreme heat, but the everyday fix for an overheating lizard is simply moving out of the sun.

items.ok_line: The same behavior that warms it in the morning cools it in the afternoon.
items.ko_line: Think about where the lizard chooses to sit, not what it does with its body.
items.exp_text: Because a lizard's temperature tracks its surroundings, it can steer that temperature simply by choosing where to sit. Once basking has pushed its body past a comfortable point, it shifts into shade, a burrow, or the cool side of a rock, and heat drains back out through its skin the same way it came in. Through the day it drifts back and forth between sun and shade, holding its temperature in a narrow band without ever generating or shedding heat internally.

items.prompt: Why does an ectotherm like a lizard need far less food than a warm-blooded animal of the same size?

options.label: It moves more slowly, so its stomach digests less
options.feedback: Slow movement does not by itself cut down on food needs; the real saving is elsewhere.

options.label: Its scales trap in body heat so none is wasted
options.feedback: Scales are not insulation for heat retention; a lizard's temperature simply follows the air around it.

options.label: It absorbs some nutrients directly through its skin
options.feedback: A reptile's skin is not built to take in food this way; digestion still happens in the gut.

options.label: It spends none of its food energy heating its own body
options.feedback: A warm-blooded animal burns a large share of every meal just to stay warm; an ectotherm skips that cost entirely.

items.ok_line: Every calorie can go toward moving and growing instead of heating.
items.ko_line: The saving is about what the body spends energy doing, not how it eats or moves.
items.exp_text: A mammal or bird burns a large part of every meal simply to hold its body above the temperature of its surroundings, hour after hour, whether it is active or resting. A lizard's body makes no such demand, since it is content to sit at whatever temperature the day provides. Nearly all the energy it does eat can go toward moving, growing and repairing instead, which is why a lizard can get by on a diet that would leave a similarly sized mammal underfed.

items.prompt: How can some snakes survive many months without eating at all?

options.label: Their slow metabolism burns through stored energy very gradually
options.feedback: With no body heat to maintain, a snake's reserves simply last far longer between meals.

options.label: They absorb moisture and nutrients from the air
options.feedback: Air carries no nutrients to absorb; a fasting snake survives purely on what it stored earlier.

options.label: They enter a state where all bodily functions fully stop
options.feedback: A fasting snake keeps breathing, circulating blood and moving; nothing in its body actually halts.

options.label: Their bodies shrink to reduce the food they need
options.feedback: A snake's frame does not shrink during a fast; its energy reserves simply dwindle inside an unchanged body.

items.ok_line: A slow burn stretches a single meal a very long way.
items.ko_line: Nothing about the snake shuts down or shrinks; think about its rate of burning fuel.
items.exp_title: A slow burn stretches a meal
items.exp_text: Because a snake spends no energy warming itself, the fuel from a single meal is drawn down at a far slower rate than a mammal would use to cover the same body. Fat stored after a large kill is released gradually, keeping the snake's cells supplied while its metabolism idles along at whatever pace the surrounding temperature allows. A snake that has just swallowed a large meal can then go without another one for a stretch of time that would leave a similarly sized warm-blooded animal in serious trouble.

items.prompt: What happens inside a snake's body during brumation, its winter dormancy?

options.label: It falls into unconsciousness that never breaks until spring
options.feedback: A brumating snake actually rouses now and then, for water or a change of shelter, rather than staying senseless the whole time.

options.label: Its metabolism drops sharply while it remains loosely aware of its surroundings
options.feedback: Everything slows rather than switches off, and the snake can still stir if conditions demand it.

options.label: Its body temperature rises to fight off the cold
options.feedback: An ectotherm's temperature simply follows the cold around it; nothing raises it artificially.

options.label: It digests a final huge meal continuously through the winter
options.feedback: A snake settling in for brumation stops eating beforehand; digestion needs warmth it will not have.

items.ko_line: The snake is not unconscious the entire time, and its temperature is not rising.
items.exp_text: During brumation a snake's metabolism drops in step with the falling temperature around it, so its heart beats rarely and it needs almost no energy to stay alive through the cold months. It is not a deep, unbroken sleep: on milder days it may stir to drink or move to a better spot before settling again. This loose, temperature-driven dormancy is what lets a snake wait out a cold season that its own body has no way to warm itself against.

items.prompt: Why does a reptile's heart rate rise on a warm day and fall on a cold one?

options.label: The heart is a separate organ unaffected by temperature
options.feedback: The heart is muscle like any other, and it follows the same temperature-driven chemistry as the rest of the body.

options.label: Warm air is harder to breathe, so the heart works to compensate
options.feedback: Breathing effort is not what drives the change; the heart itself simply runs faster in the warmth.

options.label: Heat speeds up the chemical reactions that drive every heartbeat
options.feedback: The same warmth that quickens a lizard's legs quickens the muscle cells of its heart.

options.label: The reptile grows anxious in heat, raising its pulse
options.feedback: Nothing emotional is required; heart rate here follows temperature the way any of the body's other muscles do.

items.ok_line: The heart obeys the same rule as every other muscle in the body.
items.ko_line: Look for what warmth does to the chemistry inside the heart's own cells, not to breathing or mood.
items.exp_title: A heartbeat that follows the thermometer
items.exp_text: A reptile's heart is a muscle, and its contractions rely on the same chemical reactions that speed up in warmth and slow down in the cold as any other muscle in the body. As the surrounding temperature climbs, those reactions run faster and the heart beats more often to match the rising pace of the rest of the body's chemistry. Cool the animal back down and the same reactions ease off, letting the heart settle into a slower rhythm without any separate signal telling it to.

items.prompt: Why might a lizard turn a noticeably darker shade after a cold night?

options.label: Darker skin is easier for other lizards to see
options.feedback: Visibility to others is a side effect at most; the color shift is not aimed at being seen.

options.label: The cold damages the pigment cells in its skin
options.feedback: Nothing about the change is damage; the lizard controls it and the color returns to normal later.

options.label: It is preparing to shed its old skin
options.feedback: Shedding runs on its own separate schedule and does not track the previous night's temperature.

options.label: A darker surface absorbs sunlight faster once basking begins
options.feedback: Dark surfaces take in more radiant heat than pale ones, so darkening helps the lizard warm up sooner.

items.ok_line: A darker body soaks up the morning sun faster.
items.ko_line: Think about what color has to do with absorbing heat, not with being seen or shedding.
items.exp_text: A dark surface absorbs a greater share of the sunlight that hits it than a pale one, which reflects more of that light away. Many lizards can shift pigment cells in their skin to darken it after a cold night, so that when they do bask, the body pulls in heat more quickly than paler skin would allow. Once its temperature has climbed into a comfortable range, the lizard's skin often lightens again, easing off on heat absorption it no longer needs.

items.prompt: Why does a reptile need to warm up before it can dash away from danger?

options.label: Muscle and nerve signals both run faster once the body is warm
options.feedback: Escape speed depends on how quickly nerves fire and muscles respond, and cold slows both.

options.label: It needs to fill its lungs with extra air first
options.feedback: Lung capacity is not the limiting factor here; the speed problem sits in the muscles and nerves themselves.

options.label: Its legs are physically shorter when cold
options.feedback: A reptile's limbs do not change length with temperature; only how fast they move is affected.

options.label: It is waiting for its eyes to adjust to the light
options.feedback: Eyesight is not what is holding a cold reptile back; its whole body is simply running slowly.

items.ok_line: A cold body cannot react or move at full speed.
items.ko_line: The limit is how fast nerves and muscles can fire, not eyesight, lungs or limb length.
items.exp_title: A slow body cannot outrun danger
items.exp_text: Fleeing quickly depends on nerve signals firing rapidly and muscles contracting hard the instant they arrive, and both of these processes run on the same temperature-sensitive chemistry as the rest of a reptile's body. A cold reptile's nerves fire sluggishly and its muscles respond weakly, so even a full effort produces only a slow, clumsy escape. This is why a chilled snake or lizard often relies on staying hidden rather than on speed until the sun has had time to warm it through.

items.prompt: Why might a basking lizard flatten its body and turn side-on to the sun?

options.label: To make itself look larger to rivals
options.feedback: Size display uses a different posture; a flattened, sideways stance is not a threat display.

options.label: To expose as much skin as possible to the sunlight
options.feedback: Flattening and turning broadside spreads more of the body under direct sun, taking in heat faster.

options.label: To let rainwater run off its back more easily
options.feedback: Shedding water is not helped by this posture, and it is used on dry sunny days, not rainy ones.

options.label: To press its belly against cool ground for relief
options.feedback: This posture is about catching more sun, not seeking a cooler surface underneath.

items.ok_line: More skin turned toward the sun means more heat taken in.
items.ko_line: The posture is about catching sunlight, not about looking big or staying cool.
items.exp_text: A lizard absorbs heat through its skin, so the more surface it can turn directly toward the sun, the faster its body warms. Flattening its ribs widens the body, and turning side-on rather than facing the sun head-on presents the broadest possible area to the light. Once its temperature has climbed high enough, the same lizard often turns to face the sun instead, narrowing the area exposed and slowing the rate at which it keeps heating up.
